newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian advance unit leaves for Albania.
newsitem.headline: Italian advance unit leaves for Albania.

text.p: An advance unit of Italian troops left by sea for anarchic Albania on Thursday to pave the way for a 6,000-strong multinational force amid doubts over the risks it could face and criticism of how it has been organised.

About 20 men from an Italian army pioneer regiment and a number of crack marines left the southeast port of Brindisi after dark aboard the navy transport ship Pantelleria bound for the Albanian port of Durres across the Adriatic.
Italian television showed the group, which will be the first active unit to land, checking equipment that included light machineguns on board the vessel before it slipped its moorings.

Military sources said the unit would reach Durres on Friday morning. Its task is to inspect area where the successive main landing will take place and reconnoitre the road that leads from Durres to the capital Tirana, the sources said.

The bulk of the force, the first of its kind led by Italy, is due to begin deploying next Monday on a mission to assist the delivery of relief aid to impoverished Albania, brought to the brink of collapse by an armed insurrection last month.
Its main contingent of some 2,500 Italian troops will deploy from the amphibious assault ships San Giusto and San Marco.
Italian officials in Albania said the soldiers were being given a specially prepared guide to the violence-ridden country that includes handy Albanian phrases such as "Drop the gun!"

Troops from France, Greece, Spain, Turkey and Romania are also in the force, which has U.N. Security Council approval but is being organised by a so-called "coalition of willing" nations. Austria and Denmark are also considering participation.

Italy had initially suggested Portugal would contribute but the country's Defence Minister Antonio Vitorino was quoted on Thursday as saying no soldiers would go because the conditions were not right and the risks were too great.
"I believe it is a highly risky mission, and I have doubts it can reach its military objective," Vitorino told Publico newspaper.
Criticism also came from the European Parliament, which said the European Union's 15 member states had failed to act together to tackle the Albanian crisis.
Euro-deputies complained that EU governments were putting Italy under serious domestic pressure by leaving Rome to shoulder most of the burden.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi won support late on Wednesday to send Italian troops to Albania but at the cost of a rift with his hard left allies that almost toppled his government.

The troops plan to secure Durres and the southern port of Vlore, the latter controlled by rebels, as well as Tirana airport and transport routes to protect food and medical aid. Prodi says they may have to stay for up to six months.
More than 200 people have been killed since rebels took control of the south last month in an eruption of anger following the collapse of shady get-rich-quick savings schemes.
Thousands of small arms looted from abandoned weapons depots are still on the streets and the Italian-led force has no mandate to take them out of circulation.
